kold.explanation: "Kold" means "cold". To say you feel cold, say: "Jeg fryser" (I am freezing).

kolesterol.explanation: "Kolesterol" means "cholesterol". To say you have too much of it, say: "Jeg har højt kolesterol" (I have high cholesterol).

kom nu.explanation: "Kom nu" means "come on". Literally, it is "come now". To encourage someone: "Kom nu, du kan godt!" (Come on, you can do it!). To say you do not believe what someone said: "Kom nu, det passer ikke!" (Come on, that is not true!).

kommende.explanation: "Kommende" means "upcoming". It comes from the verb "at komme" (to come). To talk about the next weekend, say: "den kommende weekend" (the coming weekend). To talk about people who will soon work with you: "mine kommende kolleger" (my future colleagues).

kommunikation.explanation: "En kommunikation" means "a communication". To say a team needs to talk and understand each other better: "Vi har brug for bedre kommunikation" (We need better communication). It comes from the verb "at kommunikere" (to communicate).

kompetent.explanation: "Kompetent" means "competent". To describe good help from someone who knows the work, say: "kompetent hjælp" (competent help).

kompleks.explanation: "Kompleks" means "complex". To describe a problem with many causes, say: "Problemet er kompleks" (The problem is complex). To say something is complicated, use "kompliceret" (complicated): "Opskriften er kompliceret" (The recipe is complicated).

komplet.explanation: "Komplet" means "complete". To say something is entirely so, use it before an adjective: "komplet umuligt" (completely impossible).

kompliceret.explanation: "Kompliceret" means "complicated". It comes from the verb "at komplicere" (to complicate). To say something is not hard, say: "Det er ikke så kompliceret" (It is not that complicated).

kompost.explanation: "En kompost" means "compost". It also means the heap or bin where scraps rot. To say where food scraps go, say: "Madaffald kommer i komposten" (Food scraps go in the compost).

koncentreret.explanation: "Koncentreret" means "focused". It comes from the verb "at koncentrere sig" (to concentrate): "Jeg koncentrerer mig" (I am concentrating). For a drink with little water in it, it means "concentrated": "koncentreret saft" (concentrated juice).

kondition.explanation: "Kondition" means "fitness". To say you are out of shape, say: "Jeg har dårlig kondition" (I am out of shape). Do not use it for the state of an object, as English "condition" can. For that, use "tilstand" (condition): "bilens tilstand" (the condition of the car).

konfetti.explanation: "Konfetti" means "confetti". This word has no article. To say you throw it at a celebration, say: "Vi kaster konfetti" (We throw confetti).

kongelig.explanation: "Kongelig" means "royal". In Denmark, a famous theater has it in its name: "Det Kongelige Teater" (The Royal Danish Theater).

konkret.explanation: "Konkret" means "concrete", as in clear and specific. To ask for a clear suggestion, say: "et konkret forslag" (a specific proposal). Do not mix it up with the building material, which is "beton" (concrete): "Muren er af beton" (The wall is made of concrete).

konkurs.explanation: "Konkurs" means "bankrupt". To say a company ran out of money and closed, say: "Firmaet gik konkurs" (The company went bankrupt). The phrase is "at gå konkurs" (to go bankrupt).

konservativ.explanation: "Konservativ" means "conservative". Denmark has a political party with this word in its name: "Det Konservative Folkeparti" (The Conservative People's Party).

konstant.explanation: "Konstant" means "constant". To say a noise never stops, say: "Der er konstant larm" (There is constant noise). To say a value does not change, say: "en konstant temperatur" (a constant temperature).

kontant.explanation: "Kontant" means "cash". To say you pay by card instead, say: "Jeg betaler med kort" (I pay by card).

kontanthjælp.explanation: "Kontanthjælp" means "welfare". In Denmark the municipality ("kommunen") pays it. It is built from "kontant" (cash) and "hjælp" (help).

korrekt.explanation: "Korrekt" means "correct". To confirm that someone has it right, say: "Det er korrekt" (That is correct).

korrupt.explanation: "Korrupt" means "corrupt". The noun is "korruption" (corruption). To say a country has this problem, say: "Der er korruption i landet" (There is corruption in the country).

kort.explanation: "Kort" means "short". To say a day is short, say: "Dagen er kort" (The day is short). Do not mix it up with "et kort" (a card or a map): "et kort over byen" (a map of the city).

kort sagt.explanation: "Kort sagt" means "in short". It is built from "kort" (short) and "sagt" (said). Literally, it is "short said".

kortvarig.explanation: "Kortvarig" means "brief". It is built from "kort" (short) and "varig" (lasting).

kostbar.explanation: "Kostbar" means "costly". To say memories matter greatly to you, say: "kostbare minder" (precious memories).

kraftig.explanation: "Kraftig" means "strong", as in powerful, such as wind, rain or a blow. To describe a heavily built body, say: "en kraftig mand" (a heavily built man). To describe someone with strong muscles, use "stærk" (strong): "Han er stærk" (He is strong).

kraftigt.explanation: "Kraftigt" means "heavily". It comes from the adjective "kraftig" (strong). To say a price or a value dropped a lot, say: "Valutaen faldt kraftigt" (The currency fell sharply).

kreativ.explanation: "Kreativ" means "creative". To say a way of solving a problem is new and clever, say: "en kreativ løsning" (a creative solution).

kreativitet.explanation: "Kreativitet" means "creativity". It is the noun for the adjective "kreativ" (creative). To say a task needs new ideas, say: "Vi har brug for kreativitet i løsningen" (We need creativity in the solution).

kredit.explanation: "En kredit" means "a credit", as in paying later. To say a shop does not let you pay later, say: "Butikken giver ikke kredit" (The shop does not give credit).

kriminalitet.explanation: "Kriminalitet" means "crime", about crime in general. To say there is little crime in a place, say: "Der er lidt kriminalitet her" (There is little crime here). To talk about one act, use "en forbrydelse" (a crime): "Tyveriet var en forbrydelse" (The theft was a crime).

kriminel.explanation: "Kriminel" means "criminal". To describe behavior that breaks the law, say: "kriminel adfærd" (criminal behavior). To name the person, use "en kriminel" (a criminal).

kristen.explanation: "Kristen" means "Christian". To name a person who follows this faith, say: "en kristen" (a Christian).

kristendom.explanation: "Kristendom" means "Christianity". It comes from the word "kristen" (Christian). This word has no article, so leave out "en": "Jeg læser om kristendom" (I am reading about Christianity).

kritik.explanation: "Kritik" means "criticism". This word has no article, so leave out "en": "Der kom meget kritik" (There was a lot of criticism).

kritisk.explanation: "Kritisk" means "critical". When you judge something carefully, use it: "kritisk tænkning" (critical thinking). When a situation is serious or dangerous, use it: "en kritisk situation" (a critical situation).

krudt.explanation: "Krudt" means "gunpowder". To say someone is not very clever, Danes say: "Han har ikke opfundet krudtet" (He did not invent gunpowder).

krydderier.explanation: "Et krydderi" means "a spice". To talk about more than one, use the plural: "Jeg køber krydderier" (I am buying spices). Do not mix it up with "en urt" (a herb): "Basilikum er en urt" (Basil is a herb).

krydret.explanation: "Krydret" means "spicy". For food that burns your mouth, like chili, use "stærk" (hot): "Maden er for stærk" (The food is too hot).

kræft.explanation: "Kræft" means "cancer". To name the kind, put the body part in front: "hudkræft" (skin cancer).

krøllet.explanation: "Krøllet" means "curly". When a shirt or a paper is not smooth, it means "wrinkled": "Skjorten er krøllet" (The shirt is wrinkled).

kul.explanation: "Kul" means "coal". To talk about charcoal for a grill, put "træ" (wood) in front: "trækul" (charcoal).

kulde.explanation: "Kulde" means "cold". To say you cannot stand the low temperature, say: "Jeg kan ikke tåle kulde" (I cannot stand the cold). To describe a thing, use "kold" (cold): "koldt vand" (cold water).

kulhydrat.explanation: "Et kulhydrat" means "a carbohydrate". To talk about carbohydrates in general, use the plural: "Brød indeholder kulhydrater" (Bread contains carbohydrates).

kulstof.explanation: "Kulstof" means "carbon". It is built from "kul" (coal) and "stof" (substance), so literally "coal stuff".

kun.explanation: "Kun" means "only". To say nobody else knows something, say: "Kun jeg ved det" (Only I know it). To say that is all you know, say: "Jeg ved kun det" (I only know that).

kundeservice.explanation: "Kundeservice" means "customer service". It is built from "en kunde" (a customer) and "service".

kundskab.explanation: "En kundskab" means "knowledge". To talk about what someone knows, use the plural: "gode kundskaber i matematik" (good knowledge of math).

kunst.explanation: "Kunst" means "art". To name one work, say "et kunstværk" (a work of art). To name the person who makes it, say "en kunstner" (an artist).

kunstig intelligens.explanation: "Kunstig intelligens" means "artificial intelligence". It is built from "kunstig" (artificial) and "intelligens" (intelligence). The short form is "AI".

kvalificeret.explanation: "Kvalificeret" means "qualified". To say a guess rests on real knowledge, say: "et kvalificeret gæt" (an informed guess).

kvalm.explanation: "Kvalm" means "nauseous". Do not use "syg" (sick) for this feeling, because it means ill with a disease: "Jeg er syg" (I am sick).

kvalme.explanation: "En kvalme" means "nausea". To say something disgusts you, say: "Det giver mig kvalme" (It makes me sick).

kvart.explanation: "Kvart" means "quarter". To talk about fifteen minutes of time, use "et kvarter" (a quarter of an hour): "Vi venter et kvarter" (We wait a quarter of an hour).

kvart i.explanation: "Kvart i" means "quarter to". To say when something starts, say: "Mødet begynder kvart i ni" (The meeting begins at a quarter to nine). Do not mix it up with "kvart over" (quarter past): "Mødet begynder kvart over ni" (The meeting begins at a quarter past nine).

kvart over.explanation: "Kvart over" means "quarter past". To say when something starts, say: "Mødet begynder kvart over ni" (The meeting begins at a quarter past nine). Do not mix it up with "kvart i" (quarter to): "Mødet begynder kvart i ni" (The meeting begins at a quarter to nine).

kvik.explanation: "Kvik" means "quick-witted". To describe speed of movement, use "hurtig" (fast): "en hurtig bil" (a fast car).

kvit.explanation: "Kvit" means "even". To say you got rid of something, use "blive kvit med" (to get rid of): "Jeg vil blive kvit med min forkølelse" (I want to get rid of my cold).

kvæg.explanation: "Kvæg" means "cattle". This word has no article, so leave out "et": "Vi har kvæg på gården" (We have cattle on the farm). To name one animal, say "en ko" (a cow) or "en tyr" (a bull).

kylling.explanation: "En kylling" means "a chicken". To talk about the meat, leave out "en": "kylling med ris" (chicken with rice).

kål.explanation: "En kål" means "a cabbage". To name a kind, put a color in front: "hvidkål" (white cabbage) or "rødkål" (red cabbage).

kær.explanation: "Kær" means "dear". To start a letter, write: "Kære Anna" (Dear Anna). To address a group, write: "Kære alle" (Dear everyone).

kærlig.explanation: "Kærlig" means "loving". To end a letter warmly, write: "Kærlig hilsen" (With love).

kærlighed.explanation: "Kærlighed" means "love". To say "I love you", use the verb "at elske" (to love): "Jeg elsker dig" (I love you).

kærnemælk.explanation: "Kærnemælk" means "buttermilk". It is built from "kærne" (churn) and "mælk" (milk).

kød.explanation: "Kød" means "meat". To name the kind, put an animal in front: "oksekød" (beef) or "svinekød" (pork).

kølig.explanation: "Kølig" means "cool". For weather that is truly cold, use "kold" (cold): "Vandet er koldt" (The water is cold).

køn.explanation: "Køn" means "pretty". To call a garden pretty, say: "Haven er køn" (The garden is pretty). Do not mix it up with "et køn" (gender): "Hvilket køn har barnet?" (What gender is the child?).

at lade.explanation: "At lade" means "to let". To say you leave something as it is, use it too: "Jeg lader nøglen ligge" (I leave the key lying there).

at lade som om.explanation: "At lade som om" means "to pretend". It is built from "at lade" (to let) and "som om" (as if). To say what someone pretends, say: "Han lader som om han sover" (He pretends he is sleeping).

at lade være.explanation: "At lade være" means "to refrain". To name what you refrain from, add "med at" (with to) and a verb: "Jeg lader være med at ryge" (I refrain from smoking). To tell someone to stop, say: "Lad være!" (Don't!).

at lande.explanation: "At lande" means "to land". The noun is "en landing" (a landing): "en blød landing" (a soft landing).

at lappe.explanation: "At lappe" means "to patch / mend". The piece you put over the hole is "en lap" (a patch).

at larme.explanation: "At larme" means "to make noise". To tell someone to stop, say: "Hold op med at larme!" (Stop making noise!).

at lave.explanation: "At lave" means "to make / to do". To say you make something, say: "Jeg laver en kage" (I am making a cake). To ask what someone is busy with, say: "Hvad laver du?" (What are you doing?).

at lave en fejl.explanation: "At lave en fejl" means "to make a mistake". To talk about mistakes in general, drop "en": "Alle laver fejl" (Everyone makes mistakes).

at lave lektier.explanation: "At lave lektier" means "to do homework". Danish says "lave" (make) where English says "do". To ask if someone has finished, say: "Har du lavet dine lektier?" (Have you done your homework?).

at lave mad.explanation: "At lave mad" means "to cook". It is built from "lave" (to make) and "mad" (food), so literally it is "to make food". To say what you cook, drop "mad": "Jeg laver pasta" (I am making pasta).

at lave om.explanation: "At lave om" means "to change / redo". To say you change a plan, add "på" (on): "Jeg laver om på planen" (I am changing the plan).

at lave sjov.explanation: "At lave sjov" means "to joke around". To say someone teases you, add "med" (with): "Hun laver sjov med mig" (She is teasing me).

at le.explanation: "At le" means "to laugh". To say you laugh at someone, add "af" (at): "Han ler af mig" (He is laughing at me).

at lede.explanation: "At lede" means "to search / lead". To say someone leads a team, say: "Hun leder holdet" (She leads the team). To say you search for something, add "efter" (for): "Vi leder efter en ny lejlighed" (We are looking for a new apartment).

at lede efter.explanation: "At lede efter" means "to look for". To say you look at something you can already see, use "at se på" (to look at): "Jeg ser på billedet" (I am looking at the picture).

at legalisere.explanation: "At legalisere" means "to legalize". To say you have a document confirmed as official, say: "at legalisere et dokument" (to have a document certified).

at lege.explanation: "At lege" means "to play". For sports and instruments, use "at spille" (to play): "Han spiller fodbold" (He plays soccer).

at legitimere.explanation: "At legitimere" means "to legitimize / show ID". To say you show who you are, add "sig" (yourself): "Du skal legitimere dig i banken" (You must show ID at the bank).

at leje.explanation: "At leje" means "to rent". To say you rent something out to someone else, use "at udleje" (to rent out): "Vi udlejer lejligheden" (We are renting out the apartment).

at lempe.explanation: "At lempe" means "to ease / relax (rules)". To say a requirement becomes less strict, say: "lempe kravene" (ease the requirements).

at lette.explanation: "At lette" means "to take off". To say something makes a task easier, use it too: "Det letter arbejdet" (That makes the work easier).

at leve.explanation: "At leve" means "to live (be alive)". To say someone is still alive, say: "Hun lever stadig" (She is still alive). To say where your home is, use "at bo" (to live somewhere): "Jeg bor i Aarhus" (I live in Aarhus).

at lide.explanation: "At lide" means "to suffer". To say what someone suffers from, add "af" (from): "Han lider af hovedpine" (He suffers from headaches). Do not mix it up with "kan lide" (like): "Jeg kan lide kaffe" (I like coffee).

at ligge.explanation: "At ligge" means "to lie (be lying)". To say where something is lying, say: "Bogen ligger på bordet" (The book is lying on the table). To say where a place is located, say: "Byen ligger ved havet" (The town is by the sea). Do not mix it up with "at lægge" (to put something down): "Jeg lægger bogen på bordet" (I put the book on the table).

at ligge syg.explanation: "At ligge syg" means "to be ill in bed". To say you are sick without lying in bed, use "at være syg" (to be sick): "Jeg er syg i dag" (I am sick today).

at ligne.explanation: "At ligne" means "to look like". To say someone resembles a person, say: "Drengen ligner sin far" (The boy looks like his father). To say how someone appears, use "at se ud" (to look): "Du ser træt ud" (You look tired).

at like.explanation: "At like" means "to like (online)". To say she likes a post, say: "Hun liker alle mine opslag" (She likes all my posts). For a person or food, use "at kunne lide" (to like): "Jeg kan lide pizza" (I like pizza).

at lindre.explanation: "At lindre" means "to relieve". To say a pill eases pain, say: "Tabletten lindrer hovedpinen" (The pill relieves the headache).

at logge ind.explanation: "At logge ind" means "to log in". To say you forgot the code you need, say: "Jeg har glemt min adgangskode" (I have forgotten my password).

at logge ud.explanation: "At logge ud" means "to log out". It is built from "at logge" (to log) and "ud" (out). To remind someone, say: "Husk at logge ud!" (Remember to log out!).
